entries.title: Chicago cop with most misconduct complaints charged with attacking woman as he faces firing
entries.summary: <p>Over his first six years as a Chicago cop, Joseph Vecchio ran with a troubled tactical unit and accrued more disciplinary complaints than any other cop.</p><p>On Thursday night, his tumultuous career was placed in serious jeopardy: The Chicago Police Board announced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/20/chicago-police-cpd-copa-vecchio-snelling" target="_blank" >he faces firing</a> in two separate disciplinary cases.</p><p>By Friday afternoon, Vecchio was in police custody, accused of brutally attacking a woman earlier this week and holding her against her will, according to a police report.</p><p>The woman was only able to escape by scaling down a third-floor balcony when Vecchio left her unattended to grab a food delivery, the report says. She told police that Vecchio had once warned her that he wouldn’t need a gun to kill her — “he could just crack her head open.”</p><p>The attack happened Tuesday, according to the report. The following day, the woman appeared before a judge who issued an emergency order of protection. The judge also issued a warrant for Vecchio’s arrest.</p><p>A police spokesperson said Vecchio surrendered at the Central District station and was charged with a felony count of aggravated domestic battery. He's expected to appear at a detention hearing Saturday, according to a spokesperson for the Cook County state's attorney's office.</p><p>Vecchio’s attorneys couldn’t be reached for comment. His father hung up on a reporter.</p><p>According to the police report and court records, Vecchio jumped on top of the woman while she was laying in bed, then punched her in the head, kneed her face and choked her with both hands inside his Northwest Side home. The woman had difficulty breathing and suffered bruising to her face and body and a cut to her upper lip, the report says.</p><p>Vecchio made her wash the bed sheets and clear out the bathroom, and he wouldn't let her leave the apartment, according to the police report. When he stepped away to get the food delivery, she jumped from the third-floor balcony to the balcony below.  </p><p>On Wednesday, a day after her escape, the woman appeared before Cook County Circuit Judge Megan Goldish.</p><p>Goldish granted the woman an order of protection and ordered Vecchio to have no contact with her, court records show. An order signed by Goldish indicated there had been prior domestic violence.</p><p>Vecchio has been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/01/16/chicago-police-cpd-joseph-vecchio-misconduct-discipline-complaints-lawsuit-snelling-traffic-stop" target="_blank" >stripped of his policing powers</a> since Oct. 7, 2025 — a day after Chicago’s police oversight chief wrote a letter to then-police Supt. entries.title: Sky's Natasha Cloud calls out offenders after sex toys thrown onto court
entries.summary: <p>The obnoxious trend of fans throwing sex toys onto WNBA courts is back.</p><p>Multiple sex toys were thrown onto the court during the third quarter of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> last-second win over the Valkyries on Friday.</p><p>Afterward, point guard Natasha Cloud, who led the Sky with 17 points, had a message for the people who keep doing it.</p><p>“Y’all lame as [expletive],” she said. “In most of these occasions, it’s men. And I want you to know that the gayest thing you can do is to go to a sex shop, buy a dildo and come to a women’s game and throw the dildo on the court.</p><p>“I’m a firm believer that anyone that has so much of a problem with a marginalized group, just come out and say that you’re a part of our group, because the hate is unwarranted. It says more about the internal struggles of the individual than it ever will say about the collective group.</p><p>“The men that are throwing it, shows that you are weak. And it says a lot about how you feel about women.</p><p>“But we don’t care. It’s a disruption of the game. Y’all lame to us. Y’all gay to us. We see it. Keep throwing them if you want to keep telling us you’re gay.”</p><p>The trend began last season, when cryptocurrency promoters took responsibility for the stunt. It resurfaced Thursday night in Los Angeles, where the person accused of throwing one onto the court was arrested and banned from the arena.</p><p>The Sky are reviewing camera footage to identify the person responsible.</p>

entries.title: Has Tyler Marsh earned a third season with the Sky?
entries.summary: <p>When Tyler Marsh stays up late thinking about the season, no single moment sticks out.</p><p>Not Rickea Jackson going down in the fourth game of the season. Not Skylar Diggins' Instagram post about being benched. Not any one of Sydney Taylor's buzzer-beaters.</p><p>For Marsh, the mental montage is all about what could have been.</p><p>"It's a culmination of the close games we were in, where it felt like we coulda won," he said.</p><p>Despite Friday night's impressive win over the title-contending Valkyries, sealed by another Taylor dagger, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> are 15-22 with virtually no shot at the playoffs — and the games earlier in the season that came down to the wire are to blame.</p><p>It's not that they haven't played good basketball this season. Their net rating — point differential per 100 possessions — sits just 1.5 points behind the Mystics, who are a lock for the playoffs. The difference has been closing.</p><p>The missed opportunities weigh on the second-year coach, especially given what the offseason promised.</p><p>"The pressure [was] more this year," he told the Sun-Times on Thursday after practice. "There are so many moves made this year. There was a picture and an idea of what this was going to look like.</p><p>"We saw moments of that early on in the year while still being down some important bodies. We started off 3-1 and didn't have Sloot and Azura. And then it was like, when someone came back, someone else went down."</p><p>Maybe the biggest indictment of the Sky's season, beyond the record, is the inconsistency. There were stretches of pesky defense and stretches of dominant offense, but the two synced up only on occasion.</p><p>Whether Marsh gets a third season comes down to how the front office reads that: as a coaching failure, or as the cost of the injuries and the moving pieces. Courtney Vandersloot, Azura Stevens and DiJonai Carrington all returned at different points, each time redirecting the flow of the team.</p><p>One thing stayed constant, though, and it's the value Marsh talks about most: selflessness. No team in the league finishes a higher share of its baskets off an assist. On Friday, nearly 80% of them were assisted.</p><p>"Tyler has done a great job of playing his players through their strengths," Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase said before the game. "He gets them moving, a lot of false action. Brings back memories when we would go at it in practice in Vegas."</p><p>Marsh, who coached alongside Nakase as an assistant in Las Vegas, often talks about how impressed he is by the way she has gotten the Valkyries' play style to mirror her hard-nosed identity. Which leaves a question for the Sky front office: Do the Sky mirror Marsh?</p><p>His players always vouch for what he's trying to be — present and consistent. They say his belief in them shows. He gives everyone a voice and lets players be themselves. On the play that won the game Friday night, the idea was simply to get it to Taylor and let her rock.</p><p>That approach has started to show up in the results.</p><p>Since the All-Star break, the Sky are 5-3 in clutch games — those within five points in the final five minutes. And with the last-second win against the Aces earlier this month, when Marsh used one of Becky Hammon's old plays against her, they've now beaten each of the league's top three teams.</p><p>That doesn't erase 22 losses, and Marsh can't claim all of the progress; Taylor's emergence as a stone-cold killer and Natasha Cloud's emotional leadership deserve credit, too.</p><p>But it does leave the front office with a harder decision than the record suggests. They'll have to decide whether the progress in the clutch and the buy-in to Marsh's selfless approach are enough to let him try again.</p>

entries.title: Slow start behind him, Alex Bregman piling up big moments, looking capable of carrying Cubs deep into October
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — The guy who was getting booed at Wrigley Field earlier this season is now looking capable of carrying the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> deep into October.</p><p>Third baseman Alex Bregman has segued from a slow start to his $175 million free-agent contract to the type of production that earns somebody that kind of money in this game.</p><p>Since beginning the season batting .235 with seven homers and just a .670 OPS in his first 92 games as a Cub, he came into Friday hitting .306 with nine homers and a .962 OPS in his last 33 games.</p><p>“The work ethic and attention to detail is probably some of the best I’ve ever seen,” catcher Carson Kelly said Friday. “With a guy like that, who’s had the success he’s had and the consistency over the years? We always look at, ‘Oh, he had a bad month,’ but you look at the end of the year at what he’s done? He continues to be that same guy. With the work ethic and the attention to detail, over time, it evens itself out.”</p><p>Those wildly improved numbers have come along with a rapid-fire sequence of signature moments for Bregman. He hit a dramatic, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/06/cubs-walk-off-win-alex-bregman-home-run-pete-crow-armstrong-stolen-base-blue-jays-dodgers-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp" >down-to-their-last-strike home run</a> to force extra innings in a Cubs win over the Blue Jays. Then he had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/12/cubs-alex-bregman-three-homers-dansby-swanson-ryan-rolison-phil-maton-knee-injury-jackson-kent-nationals" >a three-homer game</a> in a win over the Nationals. Then he drove in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/18/cubs-white-sox-crosstown-alex-bregman-pete-crow-armstrong-munetaka-murakami-kevin-gausman" >both the tying and winning runs</a> in Tuesday’s win over the White Sox.</p><p>Forget those early-season boos. Bregman is now causing deliriously happy pandemonium at Clark and Addison on a regular basis.</p><p>“I’ve seen it his whole career. He’s a special player when he’s going right,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said last week. “What’s also amazing about him, when he was grinding and everything, there were so many things he was doing to help us win games, whether it was defensively, walking guys through at-bats, showing up every day and playing.</p><p>“Now that he’s rolling and in a good spot, it’s a lot of fun to watch.”</p><p>Indeed, Bregman was brought in to do more than just hit.</p><p>He’s among the Cubs’ cadre of Gold Glove defenders and looked the part Wednesday against the White Sox, shining in the field while the team’s offense only mustered a couple hits in a shutout loss.</p><p>And Bregman, too, has repeatedly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/07/cubs-alex-bregman-home-run-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-pitcher-mlb-trade-deadline-angels" >lived up to his reputation as a behind-the-scenes aid for teammates</a>, constantly cited as someone sharing tips and insights gleaned from all his winning experience to try to give everyone on the roster an edge.</p><p>“The one thing he’s brought so much is being able to help guys navigate through things,” Swanson said, “whether it’s other guys and their at-bats, pitchers and their approach to getting other teams out. He’s best when he’s got his hands in everything.</p><p>“Just his knowledge and his perspective on the game itself has really been beneficial for our group. I’ve been able to learn from him, and we’ve all been better for it.”</p><p>Yes, such an impact is the reason the Cubs shelled out for Bregman, who would like to add to his already-impressive collection of World Series rings, two of them from his time with the Astros.</p><p>And with October on everyone’s minds — except the one-day-at-a-time Cubs, obviously — Bregman looks poised to help carry the team deep into the postseason.</p><p>Bregman has 19 homers and a .791 OPS in a whopping 102 career playoff games, including 26 in the World Series.</p><p>“The attention to detail that he has, he stays in the moment, he’s able to have a short-term memory,” Kelly said, “those are big things, especially in the postseason, when every moment feels so big.”</p><p>Combine that track record with what Cubs fans are finally seeing from the big offseason addition, and Bregman might go from early-summer disappointment to early-fall superstar.</p><p>Just like the back of his baseball card said he would.</p><p>“You can’t fake it through 162 games,” manager Craig Counsell said earlier this week. “The players come to play over 162 games, and that’s what Alex is doing. It’s a credit to how he works every single day and is just relentless with his search to be himself and be the best version of himself.”</p>

entries.title: After second-half slump, White Sox All-Star Tristan Peters credits more patient approach for return to form
entries.summary: <p>By providing excellent defense in center field and staying healthy while earning the major-league minimum, <b>Tristan Peters</b> has given the White Sox every bit the replacement for <b>Luis Robert Jr.</b> they wanted.</p><p>But it’s the .301/.354/.478 batting line in the first half that made Peters an American League All-Star. That sort of breakout results in an adjustment.</p><p>‘‘They’re just throwing me a lot more offspeed [stuff] because I hammered fastballs,’’ Peters told the Sun-Times. ‘‘Honestly, they were just pitching me well around the corners and stuff, too.’’</p><p>Given that the 26-year-old rookie never even had crushed Triple-A pitching to such a degree, the Sox weren’t stunned by Peters regressing a bit. They just hoped it would arrive more gently than a 4-for-48 skid to open the second half.</p><p>The Sox liked Peters in part because of his track record of swing decisions, but chasing pitches out of the strike zone more than 30% of the time indicated he would come down from his strong start. That he entered Friday batting .286/.388/.452 in August is owed to returning to a more patient approach.</p><p>‘‘I always like jumping the first pitch, but making that a smaller zone [is what] I’m looking for,’’ Peters said. ‘‘It’s more where I’m chasing is the bigger issue than how much chasing. If I’m chasing up, that means my approach is in the right spot.’’</p><h3>Doyle ready to make adjustments</h3><p>Despite losing Robert’s fly to center in the lights in the fourth inning, <b>Brenton Doyle’s</b> defensive <i>bona fides</i> were well-established upon his arrival at the trade deadline. But in acquiring the two-time Gold Glove winner from the Rockies to be Peters’ right-handed platoon partner, the Sox had a plan to improve Doyle’s offense.</p><p>‘‘Definitely did throw some things [at me] right away, but they’re not anything crazy substantial to where I feel uncomfortable with it,’’ said Doyle, who has moved his hands farther from his head in his setup. ‘‘Being a long and kind of lanky guy, I always thought I needed to overcompensate, staying super-tight. But I could use my long limbs as an advantage and create some more space and a little bit more torque and bat speed.’’</p><p>Outside of 23-homer season in 2024, Doyle has been a well-below-average major-league hitter. To his credit, that has made him willing to implement some changes right away.</p><p>‘‘His willingness when he got here to say, ‘I feel like what I did in ’24 I haven’t done since then, and I want to know why,’ that’s cool,’’ hitting coach <b>Derek Shomon</b> said. ‘‘There’s an open door to have some real, honest conversations.’’</p><h3>Charlotte awaits Martin, Teel</h3><p>Right-hander <b>Davis Martin</b> has two bullpen sessions scheduled (Saturday and Tuesday) before heading out to Triple-A Charlotte for a rehab assignment as he works back from a blister on his right middle finger. He might need only one rehab start.</p><p>Catcher <b>Kyle Teel</b> (sprained left ankle) is scheduled to run the bases this weekend and likely will begin a rehab assignment next week. Manager <b>Will Venable</b> didn’t promise it would be a short one.</p><p>‘‘With the injuries he’s had, kind of the stop-and-go of his year, you really just want to make sure that he’s in a good spot,’’ Venable said.</p>

entries.title: Cubs want to get Daniel Palencia back to postseason form: ‘I just want to be The Gasolina, throwing heat’
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE – <b>Daniel Palencia</b> returned to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> with his closer’s job taken.</p><p>That’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/12/cubs-jacob-webb-closer-bullpen-relief-pitcher-craig-counsell-daniel-palencia-ryan-rolison-trent-thornton" >how good righty reliever <b>Jacob Webb</b> has been</a> this season, that the fireballing right-hander Palencia steps back into the bullpen after a two-month absence recovering from elbow inflammation without claim to the ninth inning.</p><p>That doesn’t seem to be a problem, though, with Palencia saying Friday he’s open to whatever <b>Craig Counsell</b> and the team have in mind.</p><p>“I’m 100-percent open. I’m here to help my team,” Palencia said. “I’m open to every opportunity. I just want to pitch. I want to be that guy you can trust.”</p><p>The Cubs were able to trust Palencia to be eye-poppingly effective as their closer last year. He recorded 22 saves and finished the regular season with a 2.91 ERA before pitching six times in the postseason, nearly perfect in all but one outing.</p><p>With eyes on a deep October run, the Cubs would be thrilled to get that version of Palencia back, even if it’s not as the No. 1 reliever in the bullpen. Playoff pitching demands a lot more than just one guy.</p><p>“This is a player capable of pitching in big innings,” Counsell said. “We’ve got to get him back to being that pitcher.”</p><p>They’ll attempt to do it, first and foremost, by simply getting more innings under Palencia’s belt. He logged just 16 2/3 innings this season before returning Friday.</p><p>But the Cubs know what sort of weapon Palencia can be: one they’d like to unleash on opponents when the lights get their brightest.</p><p>“I’ve been growing all since last year’s playoffs,” Palencia said. “I feel like a new pitcher right now. I feel way more confident. I’ve been working a lot this offseason and during the season, during my recovery. It’s trying to be me. I don’t want to change anything. I want to keep attacking my hitters. I just want to be ‘The Gasolina,’ throwing heat.”</p><p>“The guy’s an electric arm,” lefty reliever <b>Caleb Thielbar</b> said. “We have a little over a month left until the biggest games of the year. Hopefully he can get himself into a groove and carry that into the postseason.”</p><p><b>Assad down again</b></p><p>Righty pitcher <b>Javier Assad</b> was sent to Triple-A Iowa on Friday, another tough break for a player with options.</p><p>Assad has been mostly excellent for the Cubs this season, with a 3.46 ERA in 22 trips to the mound as a starter and reliever. He’s been especially effective of late, with a 1.71 ERA since the start of July.</p><p>But having options means the team is able to shuttle him between the majors and minors and hang onto him, which they wouldn’t be able to do with other players; moving them off the roster means losing them.</p><p>“Guys like that are so much more valuable than people give them credit for,” Thielbar said of Assad. “He’s a guy that can go out there and give you a quality start and then, the next outing out of the bullpen, go out and save the entire bullpen for multiple innings. It’s not an easy role to fill.</p><p>“I feel bad for how much he’s had to jump around this year. On an old, veteran team like this, frankly, it kind of sucks being the guy with options sometimes. I feel bad for him, but he’s done a great job every time he’s come up here.”</p><p><b>Other moves</b></p><p>The Cubs added infielder <b>Gabriel Arias</b> to the active roster after claiming him on waivers Wednesday. They designated infielder <b>Owen Miller</b> for assignment to make room.</p>

entries.title: Sexual harassment claims, while deemed unfounded, may linger in downstate legislative race
entries.summary: <p>Yet another <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/20/amy-briel-laura-jackson-chris-welch-lig-investigation-harassment" >sexual harassment allegation </a>has been made against an Illinois House Democrat. But this time, the House speaker’s operation is fully supporting its incumbent.</p><p>Rep. Amy “Murri” Briel's former deputy chief of staff Laura Jackson claims that, among other things, Briel, D-Ottawa, sexually harassed her, supplied her and the campaign staff with “unlimited” amounts of Adderall and gave “bonuses in marijuana.” Jackson said she ultimately had a three-hour meeting with the Legislative Inspector General.</p><p>Before we go any further, you should know that Jackson made her claims in a 44-minute video released by Linc Strategy, a Republican consulting group that has worked for Briel’s Republican general election opponent Liz Bishop. The interview was conducted by Marjorie Kline of Wilson Grand Communications, a national Republican advertising agency.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3d0000" name="module-3d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>A district office employee in former Rep. Harry Benton’s office claimed she resigned after repeated sexual harassment by Benton, D-Plainfield, in the spring of 2023. His ultimate <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/03/plainfield-state-rep-harry-benton-resigns-amid-allegations-of-misconduct" >resignation this summer</a> set off a firestorm of criticism against House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch for waiting so long to do anything, which has metastasized into criticism of Welch’s service as House speaker.</p><p>Ironically, a Benton staffer reached out to Benton’s Republican opponent around the time of her fellow staffer’s resignation, saying via text that Benton “needs to go.” A meeting never took place, however, and that staffer, Jessica Dixon Heitman, eventually replaced Benton in the House.</p><p>According to Jackson, “Rep. Briel almost daily told me that I needed to take an older woman lover,” telling the Republican consultant Kline it was “difficult to focus on tasks while knowing that my boss has these feelings that she’s openly sharing.”</p><p>“It was probably every day that I talked to her there was something about me that was sexualized, to the point that on the night of inauguration, I stood in front of her with tears in my eyes and said that I wish that she would see me as something more than just my looks, than just physically,” Jackson said during the GOP interview.</p><p>“During the campaign, there was a lot of extreme Adderall use,” Jackson claimed in the Republican video. “I take accountability on my part for taking it, but there was also a supply of unlimited Adderall to keep us going through that campaign,” she told Kline, referencing Briel’s first Illinois House campaign in 2024.</p><p>Briel won by a slim margin of just 595 votes in 2024. Jackson told Kline that the Adderall kept coming while votes were being counted. “After that, Rep. Briel never gave me another Adderall at all, which made it very difficult for me because, yes, I was partaking.”</p><p>Jackson also claimed that Briel “would give bonuses in marijuana, up to two ounces that she would drive back from Michigan.”</p><p>Briel released a statement a day later claiming these were all disproven allegations.</p><p>“The statements in the video produced by her MAGA political operatives were previously taken to the Legislative Inspector General in 2025 and were found to be without merit. I am calling for the immediate release of the Legislative Inspector General’s report on this matter,” Briel said.</p><p>Legislative Inspector General Michael McCuskey told the Sun-Times last week that he deemed Jackson’s complaint unfounded a month after she filed it in April of last year.</p><p>Jackson has a different version of events. “[The Legislative Inspector General office] just told me that I was an at-will employee and that there wasn’t really anything that they could do for me,” she told my colleague Isabel Miller last week, adding, “I was never told that anything was unfounded or anything like that. I was just told the at-will employee part.”</p><p>The “unfounded” declaration gives the House Democrats license to move full speed ahead. The Sun-Times quoted the executive director of the House Democrats’ political operation as saying, “We will not allow a misleading political attack to distort Rep. Briel’s record or diminish our commitment to the values she has consistently fought for.”</p><p>However, the Bishop’s campaign spokesperson Steven Shearer made it clear that the Legislative Inspector General’s decision will not be accepted as the final say. “It should not be up to one man to be the cross-examiner, the judge, the jury,” Shearer said. “We’re going to let the voters be the jury on this, and they can decide how credible it is that Rep. Briel hired her twice, hired her on her campaign and then hired her as the chief of staff in her legislative office.”</p><p>If the House Republicans can raise the money, this could be one of the hottest legislative races of the fall campaign.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-520000" name="module-520000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. generators at the gas station, passing time watching DVDs in their cars or communing with neighbors over hot lunch at a local school that doubles as a community resource center. </p><p>The Chicago entries.title: Luis Robert Jr. returns to a smattering of boos — and a White Sox team that has thrived without him
entries.summary: <p>From the time he was signed as a lauded prospect in 2017 to winning a Gold Glove as a rookie for a seemingly ascendant playoff team in 2020 to the unfortunate role of being the most talented player on three consecutive 100-plus-loss teams, Luis Robert Jr. was always central to the White Sox</p><p>‘‘One of the guys I was really excited to manage, getting this job,’’ manager Will Venable said.</p><p>On Friday, Robert returned through the visitors’ entrance to Rate Field — to Sox teammates who view him warmly and to a brief tribute on the scoreboard — as an afterthought.</p><p>After acquiring Robert as a win-now move in January, the Mets are having a disastrous season that cost manager Carlos Mendoza his job. That Robert remains after the team sold at the trade deadline reflects his diminished value, largely because of the same issues that dogged his final years on the South Side.</p><p>‘‘It’s very sad,’’ Sox third baseman and close friend Miguel Vargas said. ‘‘I feel like we could have seen one of the greatest baseball players on the field if he stayed healthy.’’</p><p>For the third consecutive season, Robert has been more hurt than good. A herniated disk in his back has limited him to 49 games, and he has struggled when available. He entered Friday hitting .215/.290/.362 with seven home runs. With the Mets looking toward the future with young outfielders Carson Benge and A.J. Ewing, Robert — who used to range over from center field to steal fly balls from Eloy Jimenez — was relegated to manning left.</p><p>‘‘This season has been pretty similar to how other parts of my career have gone, where I’ve been hurt, where I’ve been off the field,’’ Robert, still only 29, said through an interpreter. ‘‘You prepare yourself all offseason to be healthy; you work on your body. For it to happen the way that it did this season, this is really disappointing.’’</p><p>A tattoo on Robert’s right knee commemorates his 2023 Silver Slugger-winning season, when his career-high 38 homers were thought to cement him as one of the premier power threats in the game and the centerpiece of the Sox’ lineup. Instead, Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery has hit more homers than Robert since that season (47 to 35), despite not debuting in the majors until July 2025.</p><p>Montgomery is only third in homers on a Sox team that leads the American League in runs per game in Robert’s absence. The Sox actually have not received huge returns from the players the Mets sent back for Robert. Ironically, it’s hard-throwing Jordan Hicks — whose contract the Red Sox also were looking to shed this winter — who has been the most useful player the Sox were able to add after moving Robert’s $20 million salary.</p><p>More so, it’s that Tristan Peters has provided stalwart defense in center and even made the AL All-Star team after being designated for assignment by the Rays and acquired by the Sox for cash over the winter. That’s really what demonstrated the wisdom in the Sox finally ceasing their efforts to revive Robert’s star potential.</p><p>But Sox players and coaches still look at Robert and see someone who was on the ground floor for the beginning of their turnaround last season and could have fit in with their fun-loving ascent to playoff contention this summer.</p><p>Assuming he could have stayed healthy, that is. He couldn’t, obviously. He hopes there are no hard feelings about it, but the smattering of boos mixed into his reception suggested otherwise.</p><p>‘‘This is a team that I was with a long time,’’ Robert said. ‘‘It will always have a special place in my heart, so I keep tabs on the results on the games, and I’m really proud to see how they’ve been performing this season. Those last few years, we didn’t get the job done the way that we wanted to. But at the same time, I can look back at it as a beautiful journey.’’</p>

entries.title: Overlooked Batavia QB Michael Vander Luitgaren throws 5 TDs in a statement win against Maine South
entries.summary: <p>The area has been loaded with multiple nationally ranked quarterbacks over the past two seasons. Jonas Williams, Trae Taylor and Johnny O’Brien garnered headlines last season. This preseason has been all about Montini’s Israel Abrams, Hersey’s Jake Nawrot and Maine South’s Jameson Purcell.</p><p>There was a kid in Batavia reading all of that hype and wondering where his name was.</p><p>The Bulldogs have built their football program with a community, not star power, and maybe that is one of the reasons senior Michael Vander Luitgaren slipped under the radar the past few weeks.</p><p>“I’m coming into the season with a big chip on my shoulder,” Vander Luitgaren said. “Not trying to diss on the other guys. They are amazing players. But I got disrespected a little bit. Today I showed why I should be considered a top quarterback in the state.”</p><p>The Wyoming recruit was sensational on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/08/20/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Friday</a> in Batavia, leading the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/10/batavia-football-ihsa" >No. 8 Bulldogs</a> to a 49-35 win against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/05/maine-south-high-school-football-ihsa" >No. 11 Maine South</a> and Purcell.</p><p>Vander Luitgaren was 28 of 34 passing for 439 yards and five touchdowns with one interception. The yardage and TDs are career-high marks.</p><p>“He is the best quarterback in Illinois,” Batavia coach Dennis Piron said. “I’m biased; I’m his coach. There are a lot of good QBs this year, but he is severely underrated. We also have dudes that can go get it and catch the ball.”</p><p>Vander Luitgaren connected with seven receivers. Darin Ashiru, a Western Michigan recruit, had 10 catches for 153 yards and 2 TDs.</p><p>“[Maine South] is a phenomenal team but keeping our foot on the gas was the key today,” Ashiru said. “Michael is like that. He’s the real deal.”</p><p>Wyoming recruit Thomas Prescott finished with five receptions for 70 yards and a TD. Brennon Zeng, an NIU recruit, added seven catches for 141 yards and two touchdowns.</p><p>“I can just throw the ball their way and they are going to make something happen,” Vander Luitgaren said. “All of them made great plays.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Vander Luitgaren has 5 TD passes and more than 400 yards so far. Just hit Zeng for another score. This was the Zeng grab that set up the TD. <br><br>Batavia leads Maine South 49-28 in the 4Q. <a href="https://t.co/OxQfoyc8Nn">pic.twitter.com/OxQfoyc8Nn</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2091004890512339235?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Maine South scored first and tied the game at 21 late in the first half on a 66-yard TD run from Syracuse recruit Matthew Schlenhardt. Batavia (1-0) scored on a six-yard run by Liam Moore to retake the lead just before halftime.</p><p>Vander Luitgaren and Prescott connected for a touchdown to open the third quarter, and the Bulldogs never looked back.</p><p>“You knew [Vander Luitgaren] was special on film,” Maine South coach Dave Inserra said. “We were really worried about his running game. You will see that as the season progresses. He really doesn’t make bad passes.”</p><p>Purcell, an Indiana recruit, was 20 of 40 passing for 157 yards. He threw two interceptions and connected with Keaton Vitel on a 44-yard TD.</p><p>“We ran the ball really well but had a few drops, which we can’t have,” Inserra said. “That is a state championship quality team. entries.title: 2 in custody after Streeterville crash following stolen vehicle stop
entries.summary: <p>A man and woman were taken into custody after a stolen vehicle they were in struck an SUV following a traffic stop, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers in a marked squad car stopped a white sedan about 5:18 p.m. Friday in the 600 block of North Lake Shore Drive.</p><p>The sedan had been reported stolen, and officers deployed a tire deflation device, puncturing a rear tire during a brief pursuit, police said.</p><p>The sedan continued north, disregarded a traffic signal and struck a green SUV, according to police.</p><p>The 35-year-old man driving the sedan and his passenger, a 23-year-old woman, both suffered minor injuries and were taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in fair condition, police said.</p><p>Responding officers took the sedan’s occupants into custody.</p><p>The 40-year-old woman driving the SUV and a 4-year-old boy, a passenger in the vehicle, also suffered minor injuries. The woman was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital and the child was taken to Lurie Children’s Hospital, both in fair condition, police said.</p><p>Charges are pending and Area 3 detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Man charged in connection with Gold Coast burglary
entries.summary: <p>A man has been charged in connection with the theft of more than $1 million in property from a Gold Coast residence last month, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers arrested Quentin Jones, 45, Wednesday and charged him with one felony count of theft of more than $1 million and one felony count of residential burglary, police said.</p><p>The investigation stems from a call police received on the afternoon of July 18 along the first block of East Scott Street. There, police met with a 23-year-old man who told them he had returned home and discovered it had been robbed, police said.</p><p>Jewelry, handbags, watches, other high-end items and a safe containing additional belongings were stolen, police said.</p><p>Video showed multiple people entering the property, police said.</p><p>Area 3 detectives recovered additional video of the people and vehicles involved and identified Jones as one of the alleged burglars.</p><p>Detectives also obtained video footage that they said showed Jones purchasing tools they believe aided in the burglary.</p><p>Police said they found that the residence had been observed for weeks before the home was invaded.</p><p>The investigation remains open as detectives search for additional suspects.</p><p>Anyone with information regarding the theft can submit an anonymous tip to CPDTip.com.<br></p>

entries.title: Matthew Boyd called for balk on pickoff try, Craig Counsell ejected in Cubs’ loss: ‘The umpire got fooled’
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE – Matthew Boyd is one of baseball’s best pickoff artists.</p><p>So why did his pickoff try Friday night get called a balk?</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> were wondering the same thing, with manager Craig Counsell in disagreement with home-plate umpire Brennan Miller to the point of getting ejected from his team’s extra-inning loss to the Mariners.</p><p>“It’s not a balk,” Counsell said after the game. “He hasn’t been called for a balk in seven years. He had one where it wasn’t a pickoff move, but he hasn’t been called for a balk in seven years.</p><p>“It’s a situation where the umpire got fooled and made up a call because he got fooled. It’s not a balk. Flat out. No other umpire is calling that a balk, hasn’t called it for seven years.”</p><p>Boyd picked 11 runners off last year, leading the major leagues and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/09/06/cubs-matthew-boyd-pickoff-record-craig-counsell-pete-crow-armstrong" >setting a new Cubs single-season franchise record</a>. He’s got four pickoffs this season, just two off the big league lead despite missing significant time with injuries.</p><p>Indeed, Boyd has been called for just one balk since he was called for four of them in 2019, coming in 2024 with the Guardians.</p><p>“He thought that I was going to the plate, to sum things up,” Boyd said. “That’s the same move I’ve done. That’s the first time that move has been called a balk since 2019, when Joe West called it front third base.”</p><p>The balk proved costly in the fifth inning.</p><p>With the Cubs down a run – they scored three times in the first inning, but Boyd allowed four runs in the second, including three on a Cal Raleigh home run – the leadoff man reached on a throwing error by Nico Hoerner, then advanced to second on the balk.</p><p>The runner moved to third when the next hitter grounded out, and he scored on a bloop single into shallow center field.</p><p>“Any run can make a difference in a game,” Boyd said. “Obviously, I would have loved to be better, would have loved to get a strikeout after [the balk]. The ground ball was after that, then the flare dropped in. It’s unfortunate.</p><p>“It’s more the Cal homer. The other ones are going to happen, the soft contact. The Cal homer, I could have done something better with. That’s a three-run mistake.</p><p>“When the boys put up three runs in the first, it’s a tough one to swallow.”</p><p>After a stellar run of starts following his return from the injured list in late June, things have been bumpier for Boyd of late. He gave up four earned runs and a season-high nine hits to the Dodgers at the beginning of the month, then seven runs and four homers in a dud against the Cardinals last weekend before allowing four earned runs Friday.</p><p>He’s allowed eight homers in his last four starts, during which he has a 6.12 ERA.</p><p>“You always want to avoid the big damage,” Boyd said. “[Big damage is] what happened tonight in that second inning, and it’s unfortunate.”</p>

entries.title: If you were your ward's alderperson for a week, what would you do? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked people what they'd do if they became their ward's alderperson for a week. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Push to trim bushes in alleys, have abandoned properties properly secured so homeless people can’t enter and set up shelter. ... Politics makes strange bedfellows."<br><i>— Brown Mike</i></p>

entries.title: Tollway hike will improve infrastructure, save commute time, boost economy
entries.summary: <p>Time is the one resource none of us can replace.</p><p>When congestion adds 20 to 30 minutes to a commute, the loss means less time with family and for everything else that matters.</p><p>That is why the Illinois Tollway’s <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2026/07/27/illinois-tollway-proposes-265-billion-capital-projects-plan-57-toll-hike-illinois" target="_blank" >Driving Connections Plan</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/19/illinois-tollway-toll-hike" >approved </a>by the agency's board Wednesday, deserves public support. The 15-year, $26.5 billion program will improve roads, bridges and interchanges across all five corridors. Carried out responsibly, it can strengthen the regional economy while returning time to Illinoisans.</p><p>We have seen what better connections can accomplish. Improvements along the Jane Addams Memorial Tollway (Interstate 90) cut some trips by about 25 minutes. The interchange connecting I-294 and I-57 saves some drivers as much as 13 minutes per trip.</p><p>For someone saving 25 minutes each way, that exceeds four hours a week. Over a 50-week working year, it is more than 200 hours — or eight days — given back.</p><p>Multiply that impact across thousands of travelers. Employees arrive more reliably. Deliveries face fewer delays. Businesses reach more customers. Parents get home sooner. Time saved on the road does not disappear; people put it to use.</p><p>Better connections can also change a community’s economic outlook. Businesses need reliable access to workers, customers, suppliers, airports and rail terminals. Unpredictable congestion adds costs and limits opportunity.</p><p>After I-90 was improved, the surrounding area recorded a $650 million increase in assessed value and added 6.4 million square feet of industrial, commercial, retail and residential development. The I-294/I-57 interchange, where two major highways once crossed without a direct connection, has opened surrounding communities to new development opportunities.</p><p>Driving Connections can build on those results. Modernizing interchanges, replacing aging infrastructure and improving traffic flow can shorten commutes, expand access to jobs and make land more attractive for development.</p><p>No project can eliminate every delay or guarantee growth. But thoughtful investments in busy corridors can create benefits lasting decades.</p><p>We should judge Driving Connections by more than miles rebuilt, bridges replaced, and yes — increased toll rates. We should ask how much time is saved by travelers, how many opportunities communities gain and whether businesses can move people and goods more reliably.</p><p>Infrastructure is about getting to work, delivering to a customer and making it home sooner.</p><p>That is time well worth investing in.</p><p><i>Kevin Artl, president and CEO, American Council of Engineering Companies of Illinois</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c60000" name="module-c60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Coach airline passengers need more bathrooms</h3><p>If airline customers were prison inmates, they would still be guaranteed greater lavatory access inside an airplane.</p><p>As outlined by <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/illinois/Ill-Admin-Code-tit-20-SS-701.80" target="_blank" >law in Illinois</a>, where United Airlines is headquartered, inmates are awarded one lavatory per eight prisoners. Yet many mid-sized flights offer coach passengers access to two or three toilets.</p><p>This absurd first-class restriction of a highly limited commodity increases coach passengers’ risks from turbulence by delaying their return to the safety of their seats. Those allowed to board early, including parents with young children or the mobility-challenged, have the same risks once the flight starts.</p><p>While I was flying inbound to Chicago recently, a terse United flight attendant forbade a neatly dressed woman sitting next to me in coach from using the front lavatory. No consideration was given either to a woman holding an infant or an elderly gentleman, both of whom balanced between the seats in the growing line for a rear restroom.</p><p>One small consolation: A man in a Marines polo was permitted to use the front facilities reserved for first-class or business-class passengers. But one has to wonder whether every armed services member has to wear military gear publicly to be treated with equal dignity on flights.</p><p>Such blatant lack of bathroom access is not acceptable by law in nearly every other industry. <a class="Link" href="https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.141" target="_blank" ><u>OSHA standards</u></a> dictate six toilet facilities be provided for 111 or more employees. In contrast, the popular Boeing 737-700, which carries a maximum of <a class="Link" href="https://www.boeing.com/commercial/737ng" target="_blank" ><u>149 passengers</u></a>, has only two to three lavatories.</p><p>First-class passengers pay for the privileges of more legroom, early boarding and a better class of snacks. But a complimentary drink does not entitle them to a private bathroom as well, while fellow passengers are forced to endure an unsafe wait for basic bodily care.</p><p>Americans have done away with kings. We would do well to ditch such royal entitlements, including private throne rooms, in our skies as well.</p><p><i>Emily Burton Sherman, Greenville, Kentucky</i> </p><h3>Trump is no Teddy Roosevelt</h3><p>I recently visited the new <a class="Link" href="https://www.trlibrary.com/" target="_blank" >Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library</a> in western North Dakota. As I read quotes from "TR" that were displayed on the library's walls, I wondered which quotes were embraced by Donald Trump, who <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-attends-theodore-roosevelt-presidential-library-dedication-ceremony" target="_blank" >attended </a>the library's opening and fancies himself as qualified to be displayed beside Roosevelt's likeness on <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-heads-mount-rushmore-kick-off-america-250/story?id=134443201" target="_blank" >Mount Rushmore</a>.</p><p>I'm sure Trump would approve of Roosevelt's belief that the United States should be an expansionist nation that would acquire territory for itself, as it had just done in the Spanish-American War, which took place a few years before Roosevelt became president, thus establishing a nascent American empire. Trump has shown such tastes with his proposals to annex Greenland and absorb Canada as the 51st state.</p><p>However, Roosevelt believed the government should determine whether corporations were acting in the public interest and break up monopolies that weren't giving what he called a "square deal" to all Americans. Contrast that with Trump's seeming view that the strong exploiting ordinary citizens is the proper order of things and that the government should not obstruct such behavior. Trump has consistently eliminated government protections for citizens against the powerful.</p><p>What likely furrowed Trump's brow — if he saw it on the library wall — was part of a Roosevelt <a class="Link" href="https://www.trlibrary.com/tr/fake-quotes" target="_blank" >quote that states</a>, "Patriotism means to stand by the country. It does not mean to stand by the president ..."</p><p>Our current president has obvious difficulty distinguishing one from the other. The government observations of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/07/03/america-july-fourth-immigrants-trump-national-anthem-oak-tree-civil-rights-racism-religion" target="_blank" >250th anniversary</a> of the Declaration of Independence undoubtedly incorporated more than a little input from the president and became, as so many things do these days, vehicles for drawing attention to Trump.</p><p>When Roosevelt wrote the words above, he showed his superior humility. He understood his place in the order of things far better than Trump does. This did not prevent Roosevelt from being far more accomplished than Trump can realistically dream of being.</p><p><i>Curt Fredrikson, Mokena</i></p><h3>Mailing it in</h3><p>Despite complaining loudly and often about mail-in voting, and while trying to eliminate or at least severely restrict it, Donald Trump, once again, <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/08/17/trump-vote-by-mail-primaries-florida-01039292" target="_blank" >voted by mail</a> in Florida's Republican primary. When asked about it, he said he was too busy with his duties to go to Florida to vote. Interesting that Trump is not too busy to frequently go to Florida, at taxpayers’ expense, to play golf and host parties for his cronies and not too busy to fly off to various places, again on the taxpayers’ nickel, to watch sporting events.</p><p><i>William P. Gottschalk, Lake Forest</i></p><h3><b>India’s arms trade with Israel may come at a cost </b></h3><p>India has <a class="Link" href="https://thediplomat.com/2024/09/4-obstacles-to-india-joining-the-un-security-council/" target="_blank" >spent decades</a> seeking a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council. A recent Amnesty International <a class="Link" href="https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/07/india-continuing-weapons-exports-to-israel-could-risk-complicity-in-ongoing-genocide-in-gaza-new-investigation/" target="_blank" >report</a> raises a question India should consider carefully: Could its military trade with Israel undermine that ambition?</p><p>Amnesty reports that Indian state-owned and private companies supplied weapons, ammunition, military components and dual-use goods to Israel after Oct. 7, 2023, as civilian casualties in Gaza grew, along with allegations of international law violations.</p><p>The report is not a judicial finding that India committed war crimes or participated in genocide. Nor does it establish that every Indian product was used in an unlawful attack.</p><p>But that is not the only relevant standard.</p><p>Governments authorizing military exports are expected to evaluate the foreseeable risk that weapons or components may contribute to violations of international humanitarian law. India should clarify what legal reviews, end-use assessments and safeguards accompanied these exports as international warnings intensified.</p><p>There is also a diplomatic cost that India underestimates.</p><p>On June 3, Germany unexpectedly <a class="Link" href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/4/did-germany-lose-its-unsc-seat-because-of-support-for-israel" target="_blank" >lost its bid</a> for a 2027–2028 Security Council seat, receiving 104 votes to Portugal’s 134 and Austria’s 131. Because the ballot was secret, the reasons behind individual government's votes cannot be established with certainty. But German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul acknowledged afterward that Germany’s position on Israel may have cost it support.</p><p>Germany’s defeat offers India a warning.</p><p>Security Council membership depends on support from other governments, including many states in Africa, Asia and Latin America where frustration with perceived Western double standards over Gaza is substantial.</p><p>India seeks far more than the temporary seat Germany lost — it aims for permanent membership and authority to help determine questions of war, peace and international security.</p><p>India, which has the <a class="Link" href="https://www.i24news.tv/en/news/middle-east/palestinian-territories/artc-palestinian-authority-backs-india-s-unsc-bid-in-hopes-of-furthering-peace-in-the-region" target="_blank" >Palestinian Authority’s support</a> for a council seat, should consider whether commercial and strategic benefits from supplying Israel’s defense sector are worth jeopardizing that larger objective.</p><p>This is not ordinary trade. It involves weapons and military material supplied during a conflict under extraordinary international legal scrutiny.</p><p>A country seeking permanent authority over international peace and security should not allow the business of weapons to weaken its claim to global leadership. India would be better served by strategic realism than by allowing a perceived civilizational affinity with Israel to compromise a far larger diplomatic objective.</p><p><i>Rasheed Ahmed, executive director, Indian American Muslim Council</i></p><h3></h3><h3>Judge brushed off animal cruelty</h3><p>What is the world coming to when video evidence shows a man repeatedly kicking a downed animal and a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/08/18/mchenry-county-judge-acquits-backyard-rodeo-steer-woodstock" >judge acquits him </a>of animal cruelty?</p><p>McHenry County Judge Justin Hansen focused on how the kicks landed and were delivered, per Sun-Times reporter Robert Herguth's story, while the steer was unable or unwilling to stand. Hansen also said "there's no indication that the animal is affected or bothered by what happened" and that "there's not a clear definition" for cruelty to animals. </p><p>Is the judge sane? </p><p>I think that an animal being kicked in the head more than 10 times qualifies as cruelty! A few day in jail would have sufficed, but the perpetrator is free. </p><p>The judge also sentenced three men to conditional discharge for ripping tails from steers.</p><p>Hansen should be removed from the bench. And this far northwest suburban rodeo should be shut down!</p><p><i>Carol Kraines, Deerfield</i></p><h3><b>ICE needs more oversight, not more power</b></h3><p>As Americans celebrate 250 years of our nation’s history, it is deeply troubling to see proposals that would give U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents even more tools to use against the public, including reported plans for <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/ice-says-electric-shock-gloves-will-curb-use-deadly-force-record-casts-rcna593122" target="_blank" >gloves capable of delivering an electrical shock</a> to people they touch.</p><p>This is beyond excessive. At a time when there are already serious concerns about the tactics and authority of ICE, the answer should be greater oversight and accountability — not expanding the agency’s ability to intimidate or physically control people.</p><p>Our democracy was built on the principle that government power must have limits. Giving federal law enforcement additional tools to use force against people, particularly without clear and stringent safeguards, runs contrary to those fundamental democratic values.</p><p>ICE needs to be reined in, not empowered with additional means of coercion. The 250th anniversary of our democracy should remind us that liberty and government accountability are worth protecting — not sacrificing.</p><p><i>Mark Warchol, Palos Hills</i></p><h3>More term limits, please</h3><p>I agree with Rich Miller that the Illinois House speaker and Senate president should have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/14/10-year-term-limit-speaker-house-senate-president-welch-madigan-harmon-rich-miller" target="_blank" >10-year term limits</a>. Every American politician should have term limits. You should not be able to spend 30-40 years in office, and you should not be allowed to serve if you're in your 90s. Change is good, and new perspectives are needed. We might have fewer corrupt politicians and those with self-serving agendas with more term limits.</p><p><i>Richard Barber, Mount Greenwood</i><br></p>

entries.title: Near West Side nonprofit offers job training and lessons that are ‘bigger than solar panels’
entries.summary: <p>The lessons at a solar industry training center on the Near West Side go beyond installing solar panels.</p><p>JIREH Workforce Solutions staff talk with students about “limiting beliefs” that hold people back, such as the misconception that someone is destined to repeat mistakes or can’t have a good career. In class, students write down their limiting beliefs, then burn them. Then they write down their “limitless beliefs.”</p><p>It’s part of a “transformation — believing in themselves and pushing themselves a little more,” Kynnée Wallace, JIREH’s executive director, said.</p><p>Founded in 2025, the nonprofit trains people for jobs in solar energy, as well as construction, carpentry and other fields. JIREH also offers career coaching, computer skills, financial literacy and more.</p><p>“Technical training alone isn't enough,” Wallace said.</p><p>That’s especially so because the program focuses on people who need more support, such as young adults from low-income communities, veterans and people involved with the criminal justice system.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div offer. He spent eight months in prison and was released in December. JIREH’s staff treat students “like family, with respect. There’s no judgment and discrimination,” Lawrence said.</p><p>JIREH means “God will provide” in Hebrew. The nonprofit is secular, but its program offers optional Bible study.<b> </b>At JIREH, Biblical principles such as being a good person, loving others and being honest are core values.</p><p>JIREH is a “safe space” where people form deeper connections, Wallace said. “People become vulnerable. I’ve seen grown men cry.”</p><p>Austin resident Charles “C.J.” Doyle didn’t know much about solar energy before April. But after the 23-year-old graduated from JIREH’s program, he started working for Hammond-based Greentech Renewables to install solar panels on homes across Illinois.</p><p>JIREH’s program is “bigger than solar panels. It prepares you for life,” Doyle said. “To better yourself, you have to be mentally ready. Nothing good in life comes easy.”</p><p>Jonathan Franklin, of Englewood, also graduated with JIREH’s first cohort. The program was “intense but challenging. It pushed me in the best way,” he said. Franklin also met mentors and successful business people — experiences that “broaden your horizons.”</p><h3>‘Bigger than solar panels’</h3><p>JIREH opened its solar training center at 1528 W. Adams St. in the West Loop on April 30. The airy 10,000-square-foot space includes a training area to work with tools and solar panels, as well as classrooms and offices.</p><p>Its free 12-week program runs five days from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m.<b> </b>Students get paid $13 an hour to take the course.</p><p>Each cohort can enroll 25 students, though JIREH expects about 20% attrition. The program’s 450 hours of classroom instruction and training include solar panel installation, introduction to power tools, first aid, CPR and Occupational Safety and Health Administration standards. The program helps them earn professional certifications in solar panel installation, construction education, safety and more.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div skills. Three others teach life skills, career readiness and other continuing education courses. Staff includes a licensed therapist.</p><p>Students must be 18 or older, have a high school degree or equivalency and be able to to lift 50 to 70 pounds. Applicants fill out an online application, then take an in-person Test of Adult Basic Education in math and reading. If they pass, they interview with JIREH staff.</p><p>Among the first cohort, nine had jobs as of early August and six are still applying. Positions include solar panel installer, technicians and sales.</p><p>Graduates are employed with companies such as Greentech Renewables, Morton Grove-based Opis Renewables and Fresh Coast Solar in Chicago.</p><p>JIREH’s strict program only allows students to be late three times or have an unexcused absence twice.</p><p>Its first cohort started with 22 students, but 15 graduated in June. There are many barriers to finishing the program.</p><p>Students often struggle with math, which they haven’t done in years.</p><p>“It was a challenge sitting in a class,” Lawrence said. “I like to be outside and in the field.”</p><p>The program offers support beyond the classroom, such as issues with transportation, housing and food insecurity.</p><p>Franklin recalled a day when his car wouldn’t start. Rob Wallace, JIREH’s chief development officer, bought a new battery and installed it in his car that day.</p><p>“They will help you with whatever challenges you have in your personal life,” Franklin said.</p><p>Kynnée Wallace persuaded the mother of one student to let him stay with her for another two weeks.</p><p>“Gas, transportation, food — anything they can help with, they’re going to find a way to make it happen,” Doyle said about the staff.</p><h3>Changing lifestyles</h3><p>JIREH’s program is not just about learning technical skills but also getting on a better path in life. “You have to change your lifestyle and mindset,” Kynnée Wallace said.</p><p>“If you’re still around some of the same people, you have to move away, especially if you’ve had a history,” she said, referring to the criminal justice system.</p><p>Kynnée Wallace and her husband, Rob, founded JIREH after working on a similar solar training program with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2024/06/28/548-foundation-create-solar-clean-energy-workers-training-program" target="_blank" >548 Foundation</a> in Chicago for about two years. She recalled one graduate of 548 Foundation’s solar training program who was killed by gun violence in Chicago last year.</p><p>Even if a graduate gets a good-paying job, they might “still be smoking weed, going to strip clubs, gambling,” she said. “It’s important to minimize those habits as much as we can. We teach them other things, like investing, putting money into a 401(k).”</p><p>West Side resident Laquan Hawthorn graduated with JIREH’s first cohort. He was released from prison in May 2023 and expects to finish probation this summer. </div><p></p><h3>Solar industry challenges</h3><p>JIREH is funded by the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity under the state’s Future Energy Jobs Act.<b> </b></p><p>It also gets philanthropic support from solar energy company Summit Ridge Energy, based in Arlington, Virginia, and the Mark Raeder Forever Foundation, which started after Summit Ridge’s co-founder Mark Raeder died in 2025.</p><p>Since launching in 2017, Summit Ridge has raised more than $7 billion to finance about 250 solar facilities across the U.S.</p><p>The U.S. solar industry has taken a hit after President Donald Trump last year passed legislation that gutted federal support for renewable energy such as solar and wind.</p><p>Under Trump’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/07/03/congress-trumps-big-beautiful-bill-what-it-means" target="_blank" >One Big Beautiful Bill Act</a>, construction on <a class="Link" federal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/01/31/sunvest-solar-renewable-energy-bram-walter" target="_blank" >tax credit</a>, or start operating by the end of 2027.</p><p>After the passage of Trump’s legislation, forecasts showed the U.S. is on track to lose up to 55 gigawatts of solar by 2030. That includes a 14% collapse in Illinois, the nation’s 10th largest solar market, according to a 2025 report from the Solar Energy Industries Association.</p><p>JIREH’s recent graduates were unaware of federal efforts to stifle solar energy.</p><p>“Why wouldn’t you want solar?” Doyle said.</p><p>Wallace said solar companies are still hiring but are more cautious. JIREH remains optimistic about solar’s long-term future as electricity demand continues to grow.</p><p>“The need for a skilled workforce did not disappear because federal policy changed,” Wallace said. Clean energy projects are financed and under construction, she added.</p><p>“Long-term infrastructure investments will require trained workers for years to come,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" JB Pritzker in 2021, Illinois outlined a goal to be fueled entirely by clean energy by 2050, though progress <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/9/22/23884382/pritzker-climate-law-clean-energy-jobs" target="_blank" >has been slow</a>.</p><p>In 2024, Illinois had 132,239 clean energy jobs across sectors, such as solar, electric vehicles, wind, battery storage and biofuels, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/energy/2025/09/24/federal-clean-energy-policies-illinois-companies" target="_blank" ><u>report from E2</u></a>, a nonpartisan business group in Washington, D.C.</p><p>Federal policy can influence the pace of projects, but employers still need electricians, solar installers, project managers and technicians, Wallace said. There are also more clean energy jobs beyond solar in battery storage, electric vehicles infrastructure, building electrification and grid modernization, she added.</p><p>“We're investing in people because workforce development has to outlast political cycles,” Wallace said.</p><p>For JIREH graduates, the program prepares them for getting a job, but it also helps create a better future for themselves and others.</p><p>With job stability, Lawrence sees himself buying a house and dropping off his two young sons at daycare.</p><p>“It’s going to be a great feeling,” he said.</p><p>As Franklin continues to apply for jobs, he’s thinking about his newborn daughter.</p><p>“Getting the best available job now will open doors for her,” he said.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Child's Baby Talk Grates on Woman's Nerves
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been seeing "Brad" for nine months. We both have children of our own. He has a daughter, and I have a son. The little girl is a few months older than my 7-year-old son. I can see myself having a family with Brad.</p><p>However, one of my biggest pet peeves is when children use baby talk. Brad's daughter seems to be doing it more and more, and it's driving me crazy! My son doesn't talk like that, and when he has, I've corrected the situation. It's not just because it's his daughter; I would feel this way with any other kid who spoke like this.</p><p>I don't think Brad notices. I have tried addressing it with his daughter by telling her that big girls don't talk that way, but it has been futile. I feel the need to bring this up with Brad, but I'm afraid my reason is not valid. I don't want to tell him, "Have her stop because she's annoying the heck out of me."</p><p>Brad has addressed some things with my son, and I've been OK with it. I think we can speak openly about our concerns in regard to each other's children. I need help with wording my dilemma without sounding like a harpy. Please help. — <i>BEYOND ANNOYED</i></p><p><b>DEAR BEYOND ANNOYED:</b> Brad's daughter uses baby talk because that is how the adults in her life have spoken to her. If they had used plain English instead, she wouldn't be speaking the way she does. I agree that you can't tell this man that what she's doing drives you up a wall. Instead, explain to him that if she does this around other children, she is likely to be teased for it and that it's time to teach her to speak properly. You can't control what her mother does, but her father could be helpful in this situation once he recognizes that it may create problems for her.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm an 82-year-old retired librarian, openly gay and a member of the Friends of the Library. The Friends group I'm active in is associated with a branch library I managed more than 50 years ago. The current branch manager is a gay man around 30 years of age. I see him at the meetings of Friends as well as when I visit the library for my own reading.</p><p>I'd be lying if I said I'm not attracted to him, but I have no romantic designs, and there's no way he would think of me in those terms. I'd like to invite him to lunch, as an act of friendship, but in view of my attraction to him (which he may be aware of), I'm afraid it may seem a little creepy. Should I ask him to lunch or just try to put him out of my mind? — <i>TORN IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR TORN:</b> You may want to believe you "have no romantic designs," but you're clearly open to the idea. Instead of a one-on-one lunch, why not invite him to a social gathering as part of a larger group? That will keep your overture friendly rather than romantic. As you get to know him better, if you find you still want more than friendship, either confess your feelings or take a step back to end the self-torture.</p>

entries.title: Three Bears with significant stakes in preseason game vs. Bengals
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — As <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> close in on the Aug. 30 deadline to cut their roster to 53 for the upcoming season, their focus is on the second- and third-string heading into their preseason game against the Bengals on Saturday. Here are three players with significant stakes:</p><p><b>WR Kaden Davis</b><br>Davis has been a training camp hero, and while that’s often a nice story in the summer that doesn’t matter once the season arrives, the Bears saw Jahdae Walker make the roster and make a big touchdown catch in the Week 16 win over the Packers. Rome Odunze said Davis consistently clocks the highest miles per hour on GPS trackers in practice.</p><p><b>RB Brittain Brown</b><br>With <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/06/expanding-bears-rb-dandre-swifts-role-all-about-creating-overwhelming-set-of-options-for-coach-ben-johnson" >D’Andre Swift</a> unlikely to play much or at all in preseason games and Kyle Monangai injured, Brown has an opportunity to showcase himself at running back and on special teams. He’ll have to be good at both to make the final roster. Brown had 37 yards and a touchdown on five carries against the Bengals last season, by the way.</p><p><b>OT Theo Benedet</b><br>It still looks like Braxton Jones will be the Bears’ starting left tackle in Week 1, but Benedet is hanging around in the competition while also fighting to be the swing tackle ahead of Jedrick Wills and Kiran Amegadjie. Time is running out, so Benedet can’t afford any lapses against the Bengals.</p>

entries.title: Driver veers into Lake Michigan near Streeterville, injuring 3
entries.summary: <p>A driver veered off Lake Shore Drive and into Lake Michigan early Saturday, injuring the vehicle's three occupants, according to Chicago police.</p><p>They all escaped the vehicle and swam to land after it crashed around 12:50 a.m. Saturday in the 800 block of North Lake Shore Drive, police said in a statement.</p><p>All three were taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in fair condition, police said. A man, 26, had a dislocated shoulder, and two 19-year-old men had minor injuries, according to police, who shared no other details.</p>
