entries.title: 4 things to watch as new CPS school year starts, from classroom cuts to enrollment counts
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools enters a new school year Monday under a cloud of uncertainty.</p><p>Last month the Chicago School Board amended the district's budget to assume the state will kick in more money to prevent layoffs and other cost-cutting measures. But those funds aren’t a sure bet.</p><p>In the meantime, schools are scrambling to bring back some laid-off staff or get by without the positions they lost. District leaders have expressed concerns about “consequences” later in the year if extra money doesn’t come through from the city or state. Enrollment dipped last year, and may fall again this year — setting up the district for more hard conversations about how it divides up resources.</p><p>At the same time, the district is about to get a new school board that could shift the balance of power and direction of the district.</p><p>Here’s a look at the four big issues WBEZ and the Chicago Sun-Times will be watching as the new school year gets underway.</p><h3><b>How are budget cuts affecting schools?</b></h3><p>At this point, parents might be confused about what students will face when classes resume on Monday. The news throughout the summer was that CPS, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/12/cps-plans-cut-teacher-positions-raise-class-sizes-shrink-723-million-deficit" target="_blank" ><u>facing a $732 million budget deficit</u></a>, was making painful cuts and laying off more than 1,000 staff.</p><p>Then the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>whole budget was turned on its head</u></a>. In late July, the school board directed the district to use $100 million to “rescind and restore” positions.</p><p>But staff have yet to be brought back and it is unclear to what degree they will. CPS says that $100 million is not enough to open up all the closed positions. The work of incorporating rehired staff into buildings is “ongoing” and district officials hope to start putting them back in place as early as this week.</p><p>So, at least initially, schools will have fewer teachers, assistant principals, technology coordinators, security staff and reading specialists to help struggling students.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-600000" name="image-600000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/00bfdfd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+39/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F63%2Fe06c83ac4723b55aeabdeac64840%2Ffirstdaycps-260825-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/161e562/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+39/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F63%2Fe06c83ac4723b55aeabdeac64840%2Ffirstdaycps-260825-11.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/52d9c6a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F63%2Fe06c83ac4723b55aeabdeac64840%2Ffirstdaycps-260825-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A sign reads "topics to write about" hangs in an elementary school classroom. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/52d9c6a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F63%2Fe06c83ac4723b55aeabdeac64840%2Ffirstdaycps-260825-11.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/146fffd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+39/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F63%2Fe06c83ac4723b55aeabdeac64840%2Ffirstdaycps-260825-11.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/52d9c6a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+39/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F73%2F63%2Fe06c83ac4723b55aeabdeac64840%2Ffirstdaycps-260825-11.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Writing materials are set up in a classroom at Revere Elementary on Friday ahead of the first day of school.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kia Banks, the president of the Chicago Principals and Administrators Association, says principals “planned all summer for how to accommodate already devastating cuts” and though they are welcoming “people back because there are needs to be filled” it’s hard to do that seamlessly.</p><p>School district officials surveyed principals who lost staff last week to find out what positions are their top priorities to rehire. Now the district is trying to find out whether displaced staff members want to return.</p><p>CPS points out that the school district currently has a “record low” teacher vacancy rate of less than 2%, which likely means a lot of the laid-off staff have already found new positions. CPS officials are only contacting staff who have not found new jobs within the school district to limit disruption. If the former staff member isn’t available to fill a needed position, CPS officials will look to hire someone else.</p><h3><b>Will budget problems interrupt the school year?</b></h3><p>The school board passed an amended budget that assumes CPS will get extra money from the state that may never come through. The board members who backed this strategy want to put pressure on the state to fork over more money before accepting cuts. They note that, by the state’s own calculations, CPS needs nearly $2 billion more a year to provide an adequate education.</p><p>But CPS Supt. Macquline King expressed grave concerns about this plan and said it could have “devastating consequences later in the school year.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7f0000" name="image-7f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1e17419/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5819x3266+0+106/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F04%2F83f19a3d455181ad24f0c754783c%2Fcpsbudgetvote-260731-038-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cf6929b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5819x3266+0+106/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F04%2F83f19a3d455181ad24f0c754783c%2Fcpsbudgetvote-260731-038-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5eb31f3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5819x3266+0+106/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F04%2F83f19a3d455181ad24f0c754783c%2Fcpsbudgetvote-260731-038-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="CPS Supt. Macquline King speaks to the school board about her proposed budget." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5eb31f3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5819x3266+0+106/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F04%2F83f19a3d455181ad24f0c754783c%2Fcpsbudgetvote-260731-038-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4b44811/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5819x3266+0+106/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F04%2F83f19a3d455181ad24f0c754783c%2Fcpsbudgetvote-260731-038-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5eb31f3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5819x3266+0+106/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F88%2F04%2F83f19a3d455181ad24f0c754783c%2Fcpsbudgetvote-260731-038-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>CPS Supt. Macquline King cautioned school board members against passing a budget in July that counted on the state to provide extra funding.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She harkened to a time a decade ago when state money fell through. Hundreds of teachers and other staff were laid off midyear and “schools across the District were thrown into chaos,” she wrote. </p><p>The circumstances were different then — the layoffs happened after then-Gov. Bruce Rauner vetoed a $215 million pension payment for CPS and many parents and teachers said the school district was too quick to adopt austerity measures.</p><p>Still, some say the board members who voted to count on extra state aid were reckless. They don’t think that a supermajority of state lawmakers will vote for additional funding during the one-week veto session in November. They also point out that lawmakers would likely want to provide more funding for all school districts so it would cost the state way more than the $100 million CPS needs.</p><p>But here’s the reality: CPS needed some outside help to make it through the year regardless of which budget got passed.</p><p>King’s original budget, the one that many board members were prepared to approve unchanged, had a $281 million hole. She and her staff said they hoped additional money would come through, most likely from the city. If nothing materialized, they said they would impose five furlough days and a midyear spending and hiring freeze.</p><p>After the board changed the budget the hole grew to $397 million.</p><p>But the district has many options before laying off staff midyear. The furloughs and the midyear freeze could be back on the table. Still, that’s unlikely to reduce students’ time in class. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/07/28/cps-reverses-course-says-no-staff-furloughs-ahead-of-budget-vote" >King originally proposed the furloughs</a> on days when students wouldn’t be in attendance.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson could again pull a record amount of money out of special taxing districts called TIFs, though CPS won’t find out until the fall when the city goes through its budget process. Last year, CPS got $552 million from a TIF surplus.</p><p>Ultimately, it’s unlikely that the mayor and school board members who didn’t want layoffs going into the school year would allow them to happen midyear at a time when they’d be even more painful.</p><h3><b>Will CPS enrollment drop again?</b></h3><p>CPS enrollment has dwindled steadily from its high of nearly 439,000 students in the 2002-2003 school year to just over 316,00 last school year. Enrollment fell last year <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/09/25/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-restarts-decrease-migrant-students-latino-immigration" target="_blank" ><u>after two years of modest gains</u></a> due to an influx of nearly 9,000 migrant students.</p><p>That growth has leveled off, but immigration policy continues to affect the district’s enrollment. </p><p>Many CPS families were affected by the Trump administration’s bruising deportation campaign last fall. Some <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/28/mather-senior-laces-up-his-soccer-shoes-again-after-months-in-immigration-detention" target="_blank" ><u>students were detained,</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/02/12/no-recess-lockdowns-less-learning-how-immigration-agents-disrupted-cps-schools-this-fall" target="_blank" ><u>federal activity around schools</u></a> stoked fear in immigrant communities. There <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/03/12/cps-should-work-to-prevent-future-attendance-drops-due-to-immigration-enforcement-community-groups-say" target="_blank" ><u>were spikes in absenteeism</u></a> among English language learners who chose to stay home during enforcement actions. Some families considered leaving the city to escape the threat.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Whether that happened will become clearer after the district releases its official enrollment count later this fall.</p><p>Last year, Latino student enrollment fell by 4.7%, while Black student enrollment dipped by 2.6%. By contrast, white and Asian American enrollment increased slightly.</p><p>Enrollment is seen as an important indicator of the district’s health. It’s also tied to how CPS allocates resources. This year, for example, the district planned to cut assistant principal positions at schools with fewer than 250 students to deal with its budget deficit. In the past, low enrollment led to school closures and consolidations.</p><p>There’s a few factors pushing the district’s enrollment down. One of the biggest: The city’s birth rate has fallen and there are fewer school-age children. In 2005, the city recorded just over 45,000 births. But that fell by more than 40% to around 27,000 in 2023. The district’s kindergarten cohort has shrunk by the thousands in recent years.</p><p>Additionally, an increasing number of families are choosing to send their children to schools outside CPS. Between 2008 and 2018, CPS served roughly 75% of the city’s school-age population. By 2023, that had fallen to 71%, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/01/20/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-cps-birth-rates-private-school-kids-first" target="_blank" ><u>according to a report</u></a> from the nonprofit advocacy group Kids First Chicago.</p><p>At the same time, the share of Chicago students enrolled in private school or classified in census data as “not enrolled” — which includes children who are homeschooled, have dropped out or are in between schools — has slightly increased.</p><h3><b>Will the fully elected school board shake things up?</b></h3><p>After decades of mayoral control and a few years in transition, Chicago’s school board soon will be <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/04/16/chicagos-school-board-election-is-coming-heres-what-to-know-and-whats-at-stake" >fully elected for the first time</a>.</p><p>It is currently split between elected and mayor-appointed members. A bloc aligned with Johnson and the Chicago Teachers Union make up a majority and so far have had the upper hand in votes.</p><p>But all 21 seats will be up for grabs in November’s elections and several interest groups, including those that represent other staff unions, the city’s business community and charter school advocates, are looking to influence the future of CPS.</p><p>This year 44 candidates are likely to appear on the ballot, including five competing in the citywide race for school board president. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/23/ctu-and-seiu-back-different-candidates-for-school-board-president-widening-rift-between-staff-unions" target="_blank" ><u>Endorsements</u></a> and political donations are rolling in. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/16/spending-in-chicago-school-board-election-exceeds-1-6-million-as-limits-lift-in-race-for-board-president" target="_blank" ><u>Millions have already been spent</u></a> in the election with three months to go.</p><p>When the new board is sworn in on Jan. 15, 2027, they’ll have a host of issues to tackle, including what to do if CPS does not get the extra funds it’s counting on from the city and state.</p><p>Several candidates have said they’d like to overhaul how the board works, especially when it comes to presenting and voting on a budget. Others have said they want to consider closing schools and evaluate whether the district should continue to increase property tax levies to the maximum allowed.</p>

entries.title: Thousands in northwest Indiana still don't have power after storms. Here's what to know.
entries.summary: <p>Northwest Indiana residents continue suffering after back-to-back storms devastated the state last week. </p><p>Winds of nearly 100 miles an hours and torrential downpours knocked down trees into people's homes and driveways and flooded basements and roads. Seven people died across Indiana. The storms caused widespread power outages in much of the state. </p><p>While power has been restored for over 300,000 Hoosiers, many residents are still without power. Gary, one of Indiana's hardest-hit cities, has the most customers in the state waiting for power to return, according to the state’s utility company NIPSCO.</p><p>Here's what to know about what The worst was caused by mature large trees crashing onto their properties. </p><p>Crews of linemen are repairing downed power lines and rebuilding destroyed electrical systems. That includes 335 damaged poles that need to be repaired or replaced and 27 outages at substations that need to be fixed before power can be restored. </p><h3>Why did ComEd restore power faster for the south suburbs?</h3><p>The same storm system that hit Indiana also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/seven-7-confirmed-tornadoes-weather-service-illinois-monday-storms" target="_blank" >caused seven tornadoes</a> in Chicago's south suburbs. Soon after the storm, ComEd was able to restore power for the vast majority of its customers.</p><p>Melody Birmingham, the group utilities president at NiSource, NIPSCO’s parent company, tried to explain Wednesday why it's taken the utility longer to restore power compared to ComEd. ComEd has four million customers, compared to NIPSCO's 500,000. That means the utility has a much larger staff and is better equipped to respond to outages faster.</p><h3>Are schools still closed? </h3><p>The damage caused by the storms caused many school districts to close schools until power is restored and debris is cleared.</p><p>Gary's schools have been closed all week. As of Thursday afternoon, <a class="Link" href="https://www.garycsc.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >Gary Community School Corporation</a> was still waiting for power to return to all of the city's schools. The school district, which is posting <a class="Link" href="https://www.garycsc.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >regular updates on its website</a>, has not said if schools will reopen next week. </p><p>In a note posted to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.hobart.k12.in.us/" target="_blank" >School City of Hobart’s website</a> Wednesday, Supt. Peggy Buffington said she anticipates schools opening on Monday. </p><h3>How have businesses been impacted? </h3><p>Many restaurants, gas stations, grocery stores, banks and small businesses across northwest Indiana were also still without power. Many businesses remain closed, while others are able to partially operate. </p><p>Gary was Chamber of Commerce president Charles Hughes said he does not have a timeline for when businesses will have power restored because NIPSCO is prioritizing hospitals and homes.</p><h3>What resources are available? </h3><p>Crews from FEMA and the Indiana Department of Homeland Security are assessing the damage across the state. </p><p>Indiana Gov. Mike Braun has activated <a class="Link" href="https://www.in.gov/dhs/emergency-management-and-preparedness/august-2026-disaster" target="_blank" >the state’s disaster relief fund</a>. People can <a class="Link" href="https://app.smartsheet.com/b/form/01a019f5a4457f0495bbef680cff9c75" target="_blank" >apply online for relief funds</a>. Immediate emergency grants are capped at $5,000. </p><p>Several community groups are also providing resources and shelter. The YWCA, 150 W. 15th Ave., is offering round-the-clock shelter, warm meals and charging stations. The Monroe Center, 4101 Washington St., is offering emergency shelter to residents whose homes were impacted. Family Life Community Center, 565 Massachusetts St., is distributing hot meals and groceries.</p><p>Capital B Gary has compiled this <a class="Link" href="https://gary.capitalbnews.org/northwest-indiana-storm-relief-resources/" target="_blank" >list of resources</a> for those in need of help, including where to get hot meals, power for their devices and emergency shelter.</p>

entries.title: Fleming brothers help lift Marist past visiting Simeon
entries.summary: <p>Marist coach Mike Fitzgerald had a funny thought while driving to school for the RedHawks' season opener.<br>His starting receiver on Saturday was his ball boy two years ago.<br>But sophomore Conor Fleming was up to the challenge, catching two touchdown passes from his junior brother Jake as Marist rolled to a 44-28 home win.<br>It was a big afternoon for one of Marist's legacy families. Their grandfather was a member of the school's first graduating class in the mid-1960s and their father Pat is the RedHawks' athletic director.<br>Jake Fleming completed 12 of 17 passes for 259 yards and three touchdowns, while Conor had five catches for 74 yards and two scores. It was the varsity starting debut for both.<br>"I was nervous going in, but after the first play it's go time so I got my nerves down," Jake Fleming said.<br>Conor Fleming got a taste of varsity sports last spring as a freshman when he played lacrosse.<br>Even so, he was "a little nervous. But I just do what I can and [I know] I'll be fine."<br>The quarterback/receiver connection is strong, as you'd expect given their family ties.<br>But they also have been working on it for a long time.<br>"Started playing football in fourth grade," Conor Fleming said. "But before that, our dad coached here so we'd be up here a lot just to be around football. When we finally got our shot, we wanted to prove something."<br>Fitzgerald liked what he saw of the duo.<br>"They seemed unfazed, cool; calm, collected," he said. :"... Both of those kids, they put the preparation in, they put the time in and that's what you love to see."<br>Marist had some other notable efforts on offense. Conor Hunt ran 28 times for 136 yards and caught a 33-yard TD pass, while Chase Tylka had two catches for 89 yards. Billy Nitsche added a 29-yard scoring run.<br>"There's a lot of things we've got to clean up just in terms of better discipline, [avoiding] personal fouls, those types of things," Fitzgerald said. "That's not who we are. That's not going to help us reach where we're trying to go."<br>Simeon had some highlights on offense and special teams. Quarterback Aki King and receiver Jalonny Billingsley (whose brother Jahleel starred at Phillips) — both sophomores — had TDs of 53 and 34 yards.<br>"I'm excited about having those two guys going forward," Wolverines coach Sinque Turner said.<br>Senior running back James Bell, whose offers include Indiana and Miami, had 12 carries for 84 yards and a touchdown.<br>"We're going to run a lot of the offense through him to set up some of the passes to Jalonny," Turner said.<br>Elijah Welch, a senior making his high school football debut, had two long kickoff returns, including an 85-yarder for a TD.<br>"He's just lightning fast," Turner said. "I don't anticipate too many teams [will] want to kick it deep if they get this tape."<br></p>

entries.title: Bears kick FG in QB Caleb Williams' only drive vs. Bengals
entries.summary: <p>CINCINNATI — Caleb Williams took the field for the first time in a game setting this year and led the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> to a field goal on their opening drive. Kicker Cairo Santos made a 45-yard kick to cap a drive in which Williams went 2-for-5 for 28 yards. </p><p>The biggest play of the drive was one Williams didn't make — he overthrew tight end Colston Loveland on what would have been a touchdown. Williams and most of the Bears' offensive starters were replaced after their lone drive of the game. Williams finished with seven snaps.</p><p>The quarterback was playing against a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/22/three-bears-with-significant-stakes-in-preseason-game-vs-bengals" target="_blank" >Bengals </a>defense made up of mostly second- and third-stringers. Bengals coach Zac Taylor said Thursday he would not play his starters.</p><p>Williams and most of the Bears' regular starters took the field Saturday night. Head coach Ben Johnson had been non-committal about Johnson playing an exhibition game, claiming he'd make the decision after the Bears and Bengals had a joint practice Thursday. Complicating matters was the fact that Tyson Bagent, the team's second-string quarterback, did not make the trip after hurting his hamstring in the preseason opener.</p><p>Johnson told the Bears' pregame show on ESPN 1000 that Williams was "prepared to play as long as he needs to for our offense."</p><p>Williams and most of the Bears' relevant offensive players sat out against the Browns. His game action Saturday mimicked what happened last year, when sat out the first preseason game and played 14 snaps in the second just three days after a joint practice against the Bills.</p><p>The Bengals thought so little of Saturday night's exhibition that they started 40-year-old third-string quarterback Josh Johnson, once played for Jim Harbaugh at the University of San Diego and posted full seasons playing in the AAF and the XFL. He's played for nearly half the teams in the NFL, 14, which is a record for quarterbacks.</p>

entries.title: Cubs’ bullpen arms ‘feeling good about themselves’ as playoff-style pitching and postseason moments loom
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE – Jacob Webb has learned something about this sport.</p><p>“In baseball,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ closer said Saturday, “you’ve got to expect the unexpected sometimes.”</p><p>Indeed, his season counts as unexpected.</p><p>The Cubs signed the righty reliever – successful, with a 3.22 ERA with three teams over the previous three years – to a one-year free-agent deal worth $1.5 million last offseason, bringing him in to be a piece of their bullpen puzzle.</p><p>But not the piece.</p><p>That’s what he’s been, though, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/12/cubs-jacob-webb-closer-bullpen-relief-pitcher-craig-counsell-daniel-palencia-ryan-rolison-trent-thornton" >the team’s go-to reliever</a>, bringing a 24-appearance scoreless streak into Saturday’s game.</p><p>“The Cubs organization is a great organization. They’ve done nothing but given me opportunities,” Webb said. “It’s been fun going into some more pressure and some more challenges throughout a baseball year. I can’t thank them enough.</p><p>“It’s pretty cool closing for the Cubs right now.”</p><p>Webb is the headliner, but the Cubs’ bullpen has been an entire group of somewhat unexpected success stories, at least in the roles they’ve assumed.</p><p>Several of the higher-profile additions from last offseason haven’t yielded what Jed Hoyer hoped as his front office looked to almost entirely rebuild the relief corps.</p><p>Righty Phil Maton has been dogged by a knee injury and hit hard when on the mound. Righty Hunter Harvey has thrown just four innings, sidelined since mid April with a triceps injury. Lefty Hoby Milner has been out nearly two months while recovering from a late-June appendectomy.</p><p>The most notable holdover from 2025, righty closer Daniel Palencia, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/21/cubs-daniel-palencia-injury-jacob-webb-closer-javier-assad-bullpen-options-caleb-thielbar-craig-counsell" >just returned from his own two-month absence</a> while battling elbow inflammation, still under the 20-inning mark on the season.</p><p>But Webb (2.21 ERA), lefty Ryan Rolison (2.86) and righty Trent Thornton (2.52) have shone while shouldering unexpectedly heavy loads, helping the Cubs to one of the top 10 bullpens in the game, the unit bringing a 3.83 ERA into Saturday.</p><p>“It’s definitely been interesting,” lefty reliever Caleb Thielbar said Friday. “It’s been fun to watch some younger guys grow a little bit this year. … You just never know when your time’s going to be up. Those kinds of moments mean a lot throughout the course of a season.”</p><p>“This bullpen’s just a testament to a grinder mentality and having fun out there,” Webb said, “not putting too much pressure on ourselves, just going out and pitching.”</p><p>The lights are about to get even brighter on these guys as the Cubs head toward the postseason, an entirely different pitching puzzle, with starters often yanked early in games and the highest-leverage situations coming at any moment, no matter the inning.</p><p>Are these Cubs relievers ready for the big time?</p><p>“Guys are feeling good, feeling good about themselves, and that’s really what you need to do going into the postseason is just feel good about what you’re doing,” Thielbar said. “It’s obviously a different animal once you get to the postseason, but going in with confidence and having an idea of what you’re doing, it goes a long way in pitching those big innings at that point in time at the end of the year.”</p><p>Though the Cubs have ridden this relief group to big things so far this season, waking up Saturday with the fifth best record in the sport, things could look a lot different in the Wrigley Field bullpen dungeon come October.</p><p>Several guys who have worked as starters this season – righties Edward Cabrera, Ben Brown, Javier Assad, Colin Rea and lefty David Peterson – could all find themselves options for Craig Counsell & Co. out of the bullpen.</p><p>But the guys who have had everything thrown at them already this season are ready for the next curveball.</p><p>“I take a lot of pride in coming out and trying to shut down whatever inning it may be,” Webb said. “It doesn’t matter if I’m in the ninth or seventh or fifth or fourth, it doesn’t matter.</p><p>“That’s ultimately all we care about is winning here. That’s the goal is to get to the postseason, and you never know what can happen in the postseason.”</p><p>It’s true. As Webb well knows, the only thing you can expect is the unexpected.</p>

entries.title: Buckle up, Chicago, it's going to be sports nirvana in October
entries.summary: <p>Vibes matter.</p><p>I know it’s only two words, but bear with a brotha. They will mean something by the end.</p><p>Meaningfulness matters. Another two words. Winning matters. Timing matters. We could go on.</p><p>White Sox, Cubs, Bears . . . matter. Now — where they are, what they have, what they’re doing and what they’re about to do — matters. October matters . . . more.</p><p>Because five weeks from now, this city will be in a projected euphoria unfelt or experienced in our lifetimes. Just witnessing (and being a part of) how insane it seems the local area codes were about the crosstown battle at Wrigley this past week, I’m not 100% (or 50%) sure the city can handle what now looks like an inevitable October.</p><p>One of the rare times in recent Chicago history where the Sox, Cubs and Bears will all be playing at the same time for something meaningful. Stakes will be high. Vibes higher.</p><p>Where every victory means something, where the timing of it all happening at the same time might be savored more than the wins. A moment in the city’s history equivalent to Al Capone deciding to cooperate with Ebony magazine to do an authorized cover story on him and publisher John Johnson hiring Mike Royko to write it.</p><p>Rainbows (either over Lake Michigan or P.U.S.H.-associated) don’t get more perfect than that.</p><p>It has been 18 years since the Sox and Cubs have entered together into any October with reason, purpose and promise. With both winning their divisions that season but both getting swept in the Division Series. And even that season, in 2008, when October hit, the Bears were 2-2 coming off a 7-9 season with no serious expectation to win or seriously compete for the title of the North. (Even in 2020, during the COVID-shortened MLB season, when both the Cubs and the Sox made the postseason, the Bears at the time were in the middle of the Matt Nagy Era of NFL mediocrity, where .500 football seemed like their grail.) Again, that ain’t what this is now or about to be in a few.</p><p>Other than those two years, even if you add the 1906 Cubs vs. Sox World Series experience to make it three occasions (or even 1917-19, when they split separate World Series appearances), you can’t because the Bears didn’t even come into existence as the Staleys until 1920. So there theoretically hasn’t been a month in the history of this city close to the one on the verge of happening after the last day of this September.</p><p>October matters.</p><p>More than it ever has. The question is, will we, Chicago as a city, province, town, metropolis, sports haven, where big shoulders and second-to-no one are our aptitude and affliction, be able to handle our upcoming future? When it hits us all at once? Making Sox pitcher Erick Fedde’s classic quote about this year’s Crosstown Classics — ‘‘Maybe us going 3-3 helped Chicago not burn down’’ — a warning because his assessment of our possible behavior didn’t even include the Bears. Who reign supreme over this city like, hell . . . Capone.</p><p>And even as the great Michael Wilbon has publicly proclaimed that he doesn’t want it to happen and wants nothing to do with a Cubs/Sox World Series, just the chase in October for both to possibly get there — along with the Bears establishing a new set precedence by possibly meeting their newfound expectations in the NFL for the opening weeks of the season — gives ‘‘Chicago poppin’ ’’ a whole different meaning.</p><p>The Bears have a very respectable chance to be 3-0 by the time October arrives. Along with a projected 90-win team in the final game of the National League wild-card series and a projected division winner waiting to see who it will play to open the American League Division Series. Meaning, the Cubs and Sox could both be playing Oct. 3 in their respective Division Series openers with the Bears undefeated atop the NFC North playing the Jets to open the month the next day.</p><p>And that’s just to start the month. Imagine what the middle or end of the month could be if all three are still in effect? With the new Bulls in the wings and Patrick Kane back on the ice for the Blackhawks.</p><p>Know this: Once this October arrives, if all are still in play, the oxygen that occupies<br>everything this city breathes will be taken over by everything Bears, Sox and Cubs. It will be different. No air will be spared. The Knicks’ oxygen in New York in June would probably pale in comparison. Our three teams versus their one in a singular meaningful sports moment? Nueva puh-leeze.</p><p>To put it into non-negotiable context: Their basketball team hadn’t won a championship in 53 years. Our October stands to be something never experienced in the 189-year history of this city. Where three legit shots at championship contention are all in play, all at once. A moment that is going to both breathe life and suck the life out of our city and the we who live here.</p><p>As no death will come after any loss in the month, only further life with an inhale of enhanced expectations. Either what can be, what will be or what is. So prepare for the best, Chicago. We’ve been waiting on this since . . . since.</p><p>October’s coming. Two words. Oxygen matters.<br></p>

entries.title: Tim Bankston, slain basketball star-turned-coach, celebrated at TF North
entries.summary: <p>Well over a hundred people gathered Saturday to pay tribute to Tim Bankston, a former South Side basketball star at Simeon who became a boys basketball coach at Thornton Fractional North High School in Calumet City.</p><p>Last month, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/29/tim-bankston-simeon-auburn-gresham-shooting" target="_blank" >Bankston was found fatally shot</a> inside a home in Auburn Gresham. Police haven't announced an arrest in the case.</p><p>"I refuse to let the darkness of your death dim the radiant light of how you lived," his daughter, Cherice Starkey, 40, told the crowd.</p><p>Mourners filled TF North's auditorium for the service before a brief fight among students broke out.</p><p>Principal Brian Rucinski, who was Bankston’s assistant coach for 12 years, said Bankston's positive influence extended beyond the basketball team.</p><p>“Coach Bankston touched every kid that walked through these halls," Rucinski said. entries.title: Bears donate $200,000 to storm recovery efforts in Indiana, Chicago suburbs
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Bears are donating $200,000 to support communities impacted by severe storms and flooding throughout Chicago's south suburbs and Northwest Indiana, the team announced Saturday.</p><p>The donation will provide $100,000 each to Catholic Charities of the Archdiocese of Chicago and Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Gary.</p><p>The funding comes as Gary and other Northwest Indiana communities continue to recover from widespread power outages following severe storms earlier this month, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/08/21/gary-storm-victims-fill-generators-at-a-gas-station-watch-dvds-in-car-eat-hot-lunch-at-a-school" target="_blank" ><u>leaving many residents to entries.title: White Sox prospects Roch Cholowsky, Billy Carlson done for 2026
entries.summary: <p>The season is over early for two of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ top prospects.</p><p>On Saturday, the Sox announced infielders <b>Roch Cholowsky </b>and <b>Billy Carlson </b>are done for 2026. Cholowsky, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/11/white-sox-select-roch-cholowsky-with-first-overall-pick-in-mlb-draft" >first overall pick</a> in the July draft, is being shelved with right wrist soreness. Carlson, the 10th choice in 2015, has a skin infection on his left leg.</p><p>Inked to a record $10.35 million signing bonus, Cholowsky was at High-A Winston-Salem and got off to a slow start in his professional career, slashing .167/.326/.333 in nine games. His final game of the year was last Saturday, and he had just one hit in his last five contests.</p><p>At Low-A Kannapolis, Carlson slashed .256/.388/.338 in 57 games. His last game of 2026 was Aug. 9.</p><p>Per MLB Pipeline, Cholowsky is the Sox’ top prospect and 11th-best in baseball after a stellar career at UCLA. Carlson, regarded as one of the best fielders in the minors, is the Sox’ No. 3 prospect and 62nd overall.</p><p>Both Winston-Salem and Kannapolis have two weeks left in their respective seasons.</p><h2><b>Catching an update</b></h2><p>Catcher <b>Kyle Teel </b>(left ankle sprain) ran the bases Saturday. Sox manager <b>Will Venable </b>said Teel “got to as close to top speed as you probably can” in his situation, but cautioned that the young catcher will have to repeat the running to be cleared for a rehab assignment.</p><p>Before coming back to the Sox, Teel won’t necessarily have to run at his top speed. Instead, he’ll need to show he can run consistently pain-free and without incident.</p><p>“You just want to make sure that he's healthy and ready to go and speed is one indicator that he is,” Venable said of Teel, who’s played only 19 major-league games this year and been plagued by hamstring, knee and ankle problems.</p><p>If Teel returns to health, the Sox could carry three catchers when the roster expands to 28 on Sept. 1. But Venable wasn’t ready to finalize the roster build for over a week from now.</p><p>“It still just feels like there’s so long to go before you get there and things change so you don’t want to commit to any one idea knowing how fluid this whole thing is,” Venable said. “Certainly, carrying three catchers is an option.”</p><p>Fellow injured catcher <b>Joey Bart </b>(broken left hand) joined Teel for the workout. Venable said Bart’s splint will be coming off “in the coming days” and then he’ll begin baseball activities. Bart has been running and staying active while wearing the splint.</p><h2><b>Ringing endorsement</b></h2><p>Sox chairman <b>Jerry Reinsdorf </b>presented outfielder <b>Tristan Peters </b>with a ring to commemorate hitting for the cycle. Peters accomplished the feat July 10, becoming the seventh Sox player to do so and first since <b>Jose Abreu </b>in 2017.</p><p>“Enjoy it, wear it [and] maybe you’ll do it again,” Reinsdorf told Peters in a video the team posted to social media.</p><p>In 2017, Reinsdorf also gave Abreu a ring after he hit for the cycle.</p><h2><b>More on Martin</b></h2><p>Starting pitcher <b>Davis Martin </b>(blister) threw a bullpen session of around 35-40 pitches. Though it went well, Venable said Martin could throw another bullpen session Tuesday before starting his rehab assignment.</p>
